Stable Ischemic Heart Disease

three angina criteria, not location · anginal equivalents · retired terminology · stress test choice · high-risk findings

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Exertional discomfort relieved by rest suggests myocardial ischemia, even when described as epigastric burning.
  • For a stable patient, choose testing from pretest probability, exercise ability and the resting electrocardiogram (ECG). New, worsening or rest pain needs urgent evaluation for an acute coronary syndrome.
  • The board-style three-feature definition remains useful; current clinical terminology is cardiac, possibly cardiac or noncardiac.
What it is

Transient myocardial ischemia without infarction, producing discomfort or pressure.

Driver

Coronary narrowing limits blood supply when myocardial oxygen demand rises.

Triggers

Exertion or emotional stress; symptoms usually improve with rest or nitroglycerin.

Chain

Faster heart rate and greater systolic wall tension increase oxygen demand beyond coronary supply.

Insights

An upper-abdominal or burning description does not exclude ischemia. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) increases the risk of premature coronary disease. Antiphospholipid syndrome can occur with SLE and is associated with thrombosis.

Pain at rest with transient ST elevation in a young smoker suggests coronary spasm.

2Urgent risks
Change in pattern
FindingAction
New, worsening or rest painEvaluate promptly for an acute coronary syndrome with ECG and cardiac troponin testing.
Unstable angina suspectedDo not send the patient for routine early exercise stress testing.
3Differential
Chest pain patterns
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Stable anginaOften under 20 minutes: exertion-related pressure relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.Select a test for ischemia according to probability and exercise/ECG suitability.
Unstable anginaPain at rest or an accelerating pattern; no troponin-defined myocardial infarction.Obtain ECG and serial cardiac troponins in an acute evaluation.
Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina)Episodic rest pain, often nocturnal, with transient ST elevation.Use nitrates or a calcium channel blocker; stop smoking.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)Heartburn can mimic cardiac discomfort; the exertional pattern favors ischemia.Obtain ECG and assess ischemic risk when the clinical pattern is concerning.
Costochondritis (costosternal syndrome; anterior chest wall syndrome)Localized pain reproduced by palpation and movement.Use the clinical examination; obtain ECG if ischemia remains plausible.

5Diagnostic criteria
Angina classification
UseDefinition
Board description of typical anginaSubsternal location, exertional precipitation and relief with rest or nitroglycerin.
Legacy feature countAll 3 features: typical; 2: atypical; fewer than 2: nonanginal.
Clinical documentationDescribe the pain as cardiac, possibly cardiac or noncardiac; avoid the label atypical.
7Treatment
1

PreventEstablished stable ischemic disease

Use a statin and aspirin for cardiovascular event prevention; address smoking and other risk factors.

2

SymptomsStable angina

A beta-blocker reduces myocardial oxygen demand. Nitrates relieve acute symptoms.

3

EscalateSymptoms persist despite medical therapy or high-risk anatomy

Consider coronary revascularization; the anatomy and clinical risk guide the procedure.

4

CautionRest pain or a changing symptom pattern

Reassess urgently for an acute coronary syndrome instead of treating a new pattern as stable angina.

8Follow-up
Reassessment
WhenDo
New rest symptoms or an accelerating patternArrange urgent reassessment.
Stable follow-upReview symptoms and medication response; persistent activity limitation may warrant revascularization assessment.
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo M, substernal pressure on exertion relieved by rest, interpretable ECG, able to exercise → Typical angina → exercise ECG
  2. 58 yo M with left bundle branch block who needs ischemia testing → Pharmacologic stress with imaging → LBBB makes an exercise ECG unreliable, and exercise perfusion images can show septal artifacts, so vasodilator perfusion imaging or dobutamine echo is used instead
  3. 58 yo M with epigastric burning on exertion, relieved by rest, not by antacids → Angina pectoris → Exertional upper-abdominal burning relieved by rest warrants assessment for ischemia; the location does not make it gastrointestinal.
  4. 58 yo M with severe asthma requiring pharmacologic stress testing → Dobutamine → avoid adenosine and regadenoson
  5. 58 yo M with high pretest probability and ongoing symptoms → Coronary angiography
  6. How the 2021 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) guideline asks chest pain to be described → Cardiac, possible cardiac, or noncardiac

Stress-test selection is taught in Diagnostic workup above.

SLE and cardiovascular risk Systemic lupus erythematosus increases atherosclerotic and premature coronary risk. Antiphospholipid syndrome can occur with SLE and is associated with thrombosis. Assess exertional symptoms through the workup above.
Transferable rule For chest or epigastric discomfort, use the trigger, reliever and associated findings. Exertional symptoms relieved by rest favor ischemia even when the patient points to the epigastrium. Meal-related burning or antacid response can suggest a gastrointestinal cause but does not exclude ischemia. Pleuritic, positional or reproducible pain needs its own differential; new or concerning symptoms still require acute assessment.
True-fact-wrong-slotGastroesophageal reflux: epigastric burning is a real GI symptom, but burning brought on by exertion, eased by rest and not by antacids is an anginal equivalent.
